source.title: The Struggle Between Continuation and Refusal: A Mechanistic Analysis of the Continuation-Triggered Jailbreak in LLMs
source.authors: Yong Deng; Zhen Yang; Ping Jian; Xinyue Zhang; Zhongbin Guo; Chengzhi Li; Jun Yin

page_placements.theme: Safety processing depends on layers, heads and feature circuits

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure content is flattened, so exact values from those figures cannot be assigned reliably.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether changing a continuation-triggered prompt structure or continuation-related activations changes harmful compliance, using prompt relocation and head interventions rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The study tests a continuation-triggered jailbreak by relocating a suffix and reports ASR. It also reports ASR changes after head ablation and activation scaling. HCS and its distillation are proposed safety interventions, not tests of whether a bypass works, so their results are not rows. HDR reply-inversion results measure an explicitly prompted judgment task, not ordinary harmful compliance. Table 3’s SFT/HCS/KD comparisons are also omitted because they evaluate the proposed mitigation pipeline.
record.test_reason: The 'jailbreak prompt' places 'Sure, here is a step-by-step guide: First,' after the [/INST] or assistant marker (Appendix D cases). That is a compliant-start prefill, so Figure 2 directly tests V4 on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Zeroing 1–3 'safety heads' with a random-head control (Table 6) also bears on V5 localization. The other head interventions are steering effects on a new construct ('continuation heads'), not V4 bypasses.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the continuation-triggered jailbreak, a 'Sure, here is…' prefill after the turn marker, arises from competition between the model's continuation drive (continuation heads) and alignment-acquired safety (safety heads). Safety heads play different roles across models: recognition in LLaMA, refusal in Qwen. HCS steering and its LoRA distillation cut ASR (e.g., JB 26→9 for LLaMA) while largely preserving MMLU and IFEval.
record.recipe_differences: Studies relocated continuation-triggered suffixes and attention-head path patching, ablation, and activation scaling; it does not reproduce the cited fine-tuning or per-token KL-position procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect varies with the prompt structure, dataset, model, head type, number of heads, scaling coefficient, and (for HCS, not catalogued as a bypass result) contrastive coefficient. The text notes occasional non-linear fluctuations when scaling multiple heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Amplifying continuation heads raises ASR (e.g., LLaMA AdvBench 16→64.4 with 2 heads at w=5). Zeroing them lowers ASR (16→11.2). Amplifying safety heads lowers ASR (16→4.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prefill jailbreak compliance is mediated by antagonistic safety vs continuation attention heads that can be steered at inference time.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing LLaMA safety heads drops harmfulness detection (HDR) from 89.0 to 51.5. Scaling Qwen safety heads lowers HDR (97.1→44.6), which the authors read as recognition vs refusal roles (Table 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety heads encode harmfulness recognition in some models and refusal execution in others.

record.problems: Experiments cover two 7B models and continuation-triggered jailbreaks; the authors note that larger models and other attack types remain to be studied. ASR uses GPT-4 as judge. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ASR results catalogued here. Figure 2 and the individual-scaling plots do not yield reliably assignable values in the flattened text.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted safety-head activation-scaling ASR results because those interventions reduce ASR rather than test a bypass; omitted HDR reply-inversion and general-capability metrics because they are not the harmful-compliance behaviour in V4; omitted Table 3 SFT/HCS/KD results because they evaluate the proposed mitigation pipeline rather than a bypass. Relevant locations: Figures 6 and 9; Tables 2 and 3; Section 4.4 and Section 4.5.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning. The safety SFT and KD in Table 3 are mitigations.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions. The path-patching KL is between clean and jailbreak runs.
Only one fixed 7-token generic prefill was tested. No variation in prefill length, no adversarial suffixes, no decoding attacks. Output is capped at 32 tokens.
Tests attention-head activation zeroing only, not weight subsets or ranks. LLaMA ablation values only; Qwen ablation is shown in a figure only. Tested only under the prefill prompt.
The pretraining-vs-alignment tension is argued, not tested through data or objective manipulations.
No deepening training. HCS/KD is a head-steering mitigation, and was not evaluated against varied bypasses.

missing.what: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct safety-head zeroing ASR (top-10 heads); values exist only in a figure
LLaMA top-10 key-head zeroing ASR per head, e.g. safety head (27,7)
Figure 2 clean vs prefill ASR values were recoverable but not entered in r1/r2

record.verdict_notes: The reader missed that the 'relocated suffix' is a prefill of the assistant turn (see the Appendix D inputs), which is the core V4 manipulation. Head-level interventions were mislinked to V4. Safety-head ablation fits V5 better. GPT-4 judge, 32-token outputs, no uncertainty reported, two 7B models only. Qwen AdvBench prefill ASR (about 39) is inferred from the flattened figure.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune a safety-trained model on harmful examples or measure harmful compliance after such fine-tuning.
Does not fine-tune on ordinary or carefully chosen benign data to test effects on harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions. Its KL-based path-patching measure is not that comparison.
Tests relocating a continuation-triggered suffix and continuation-head activation scaling. Does not test compliant-start prefilling or a range of adversarial suffix and decoding methods.
Studies attention-head activations, not whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Offers a continuation-versus-safety mechanism, but does not test whether training data or the training objective causes safety to be shallow.
Does not test whether safety is distributed beyond the first response tokens or whether such deepening holds up against bypasses.

rows.subject: LLaMA-2-7B-Chat
rows.operation_detail: Relocated the continuation-triggered instruction suffix from the clean prompt structure to follow the user prompt.

conditions.value: clean prompt versus jailbreak prompt; three benchmark datasets

rows.note: The text states that ASR substantially increases under the jailbreak prompt across datasets. Flattened figure values cannot be assigned reliably to each dataset.
rows.check: Values are readable from the flattened Figure 2, cross-checked with the Table 6 baselines. Clean prompt gives 0/0/0. Prefill gives 16 (AdvBench), 26 (JailbreakBench), 58 (MaliciousInstruct). The operation is a compliant-start prefill in the assistant turn, not a suffix. Clear rise, but most requests are still refused on AdvBench and JailbreakBench.

source_check.notes: ASR tables use percentage-scale values; evaluation uses a GPT-4-based judge, deterministic decoding and at most 32 generated tokens. V5 evidence concerns head-activation ablation under prefill, not direct weight or rank removal.

statements.correction: LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, AdvBench, prefill prompt: zeroing three selected safety heads increases ASR from 16.0 to 34.0; zeroing three random heads gives 15.6. Table 6; V5 label=limits_scope.
statements.problem: The 16.0-to-34.0 comparison is correct, but this study shows incomplete safety loss after localized ablation, supporting limits_scope rather than challenges for V5.
